newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican markets seen weathering U.S. Fed increase.
newsitem.headline: Mexican markets seen weathering U.S. Fed increase.

text.p: Mexico's financial markets will weather Tuesday's 25 basis point increase in the U.S. federal funds rate, but a series of U.S. rates rises could present a different story, analysts said.
"My impression is that the foreign exchange market had discounted or already accounted for this movement of 25 basis points," ING Barings economist Sergio Martin said.
"If it had been greater, a half a point, that could have had some negative impact on both the exchange rate and on interest rates."
The U.S. Federal Reserve raised interest rates on Tuesday for the first time since February 1995.
The 25 basis point increase in the federal funds rate brought it to 5.5 percent and was aimed at keeping inflationary pressures from building.

Mexico's bellwether one-month Cetes rate had already risen by 458 basis points at the two primary auctions in mid-March on concerns the Fed would bump up rates. Those concerns were digested and, at the last two auctions, the same bellwether rate fell 258 basis points.

J.P. Morgan noted in a recent study that every 25 basis point increase in U.S. rates adds 100 basis points to Mexican rates. It noted that models suggest the Mexican market had already over-discounted the 25 basis point increase.
But many economists are saying the increase could be the first in a new cycle of tightening by the Federal Reserve that could push U.S. rates up by as much as 100 basis points.
"If that cycle appears, of course the trend will affect Mexican markets," Martin said.

The financial markets of the two countries are closely tied. In 1994, a string of U.S. interest rate rises led to a gradual outflow of foreign capital that, coupled with political turbulence in Mexico, led to the peso devaluation later that year.
But economists are saying that this time is different.
"There is no doubt that the market could adjust a little, but the situation is totally different (than in 1994)," said Gerardo Copca, assistant director of analysis for Valores Finamex.
"Mexico's economy is continuing to consolidate. Interest rates are close to 20 percent and inflation is moving down."
The Fed called its move a "prudent step" to extend the economic expansion in the U.S.
Economists note that any continued strength in the U.S. economy will have a positive effect on the Mexican economy.

"The vast majority of Mexican exports go to the U.S., more than the other major Latin American economies. Rate hikes, but in a fairly stable fashion, and stable inflation but fairly decent U.S growth, that would be the best outlook for Mexico," said Richard Segal, economist with Santander Investments.
Traders noted the Mexican peso closed more or less stable after the news the rate rise was in line with expectations.
The Mexican bolsa ended up on the day, while the same-day Cetes ended down 60 basis points to 21.40 percent.
